questions.question: Which dynasty ruled over Kannauj during the Tripartite Struggle?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gurjara-Pratiharas**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Tripartite Struggle** was a significant historical conflict that took place in **North India** between the **8th century** and the **10th century**.
 
• The struggle was centered around the control of the city of **Kannauj**, which was considered a symbol of prestige and sovereign power after the death of **Harshavardhana**.
 
• Three major dynasties were involved in this long-standing conflict: the **Gurjara-Pratiharas** of **Western India**, the **Palas** of **Bengal**, and the **Rashtrakutas** of the **Deccan**.
 
• The **Gurjara-Pratiharas** ultimately managed to establish long-term control over **Kannauj**. During the reign of **Nagabhata II** (around **816 AD**), the dynasty successfully conquered **Kannauj** and made it their **capital** city. ***Hence, the Gurjara-Pratiharas are the correct answer as they ruled over Kannauj as their primary seat of power during this era.***
 
• The conflict initially began when the **Pratihara** king **Vatsaraja** defeated the **Pala** ruler **Dharmapala** and the **Rashtrakuta** king **Dhruva Dharavarsha** intervened, defeating both.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Significance of Kannauj:**

 
 
• Located in the **Ganga valley** in present-day **Uttar Pradesh**, **Kannauj** was strategically important for trade and agriculture.
 
• Possession of **Kannauj** signified lordship over the **Indo-Gangetic plains**, leading to its nickname as the **"Mahodaya Nagar"**.
 
 
 
• **The Palas:**
 
 
• Founded by **Gopala** in **750 AD**, this dynasty ruled over **Bengal** and **Bihar**.
 
• **Dharmapala** and **Devapala** were the most powerful rulers who briefly installed their nominees on the throne of **Kannauj** during the struggle.
 
 
 
• **The Rashtrakutas:**
 
 
• Founded by **Dantidurga** in **753 AD** with their capital at **Manyakheta** in the **Deccan** region (modern-day **Karnataka**).
 
• Rulers like **Dhruva**, **Govinda III**, and **Indra III** frequently invaded **North India** and defeated the **Pratiharas** and **Palas**, but they often returned south, allowing the **Pratiharas** to regain control.
 
 
 
• **The Chalukyas and Cholas:**
 
 
• The **Chalukyas** of **Badami** had declined by the mid-**8th century**, and the **Chalukyas** of **Kalyani** rose later; they were not primary participants in the **Tripartite Struggle**.
 
• The **Cholas** were a powerful maritime empire in **South India** that reached its peak under **Rajaraja I** and **Rajendra I** in the **11th century**, well after the core period of the **Tripartite Struggle**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Consequences of the Struggle:**

 
 
• The constant warfare for over **two centuries** exhausted the resources of all three dynasties, leading to their eventual fragmentation and decline.
 
• The weakness of these empires paved the way for the rise of small **Rajput** principalities and later facilitated the **Ghaznavid** and **Ghurid** invasions of **India**.
 
 
 
• **Mihira Bhoja:**
 
 
• The **Gurjara-Pratihara** ruler **Mihira Bhoja** (**836–885 AD**) was one of the most formidable monarchs of this period. He consolidated **Kannauj** and successfully defended his territory against both the **Palas** and the **Rashtrakutas**.
 
• The **Arab** traveler **Al-Masudi** referred to the **Gurjara-Pratihara** kingdom as **Al-Juzr** and praised their powerful cavalry.

**Statements: **

Some ants are lizards.

All lizards are spiders.

No spider is a rat.

**Conclusions:**

(I) Some rats are lizards.

(II) Some spiders are ants.

questions.question: The product of two numbers, X and Y, is 6760, and the HCF of X and Y is 13. Find the number of possible pairs (X,Y), given that X > Y.
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

⇒ X = 13a, Y = 13b and HCF(a,b) = 1

⇒ XY = 6760 ⇒ 169ab = 6760 ⇒ ab = 40

⇒ Prime factor: 40 = 2³ × 5

⇒ Coprime pairs ⇒ assign full powers: (1,40), (5,8)

⇒ With X > Y ⇒ (40,1), (8,5) ⇒ total 2 pairs

**∴ Answer = 2**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** XY = 6760, HCF = 13

**Formula:** X = 13a, Y = 13b, where HCF(a,b) = 1

⇒ XY = 169ab = 6760

⇒ ab = 6760 / 169 = 40

⇒ Factors of 40: (1,40), (2,20), (4,10), (5,8)

⇒ Coprime pairs:

⇒ (1,40), (5,8)

⇒ Since X > Y:

⇒ (a,b) = (40,1), (8,5)

⇒ Total possible pairs = 2

**∴ Final Answer = 2**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

**HCF Form:** X = HCF × a, Y = HCF × b

**Product Rule:** XY = HCF² × ab

**Coprime Condition:** HCF(a,b) = 1

**Counting Trick:** Distribute prime powers fully to keep coprime

questions.question: As per Article ___________ of the Indian Constitution, from the date of commencement of the Constitution (Sixty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1991, the Union territory of Delhi shall be called the National Capital Territory of Delhi.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**239AA**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 239AA** of the **Indian Constitution** was inserted by the **Constitution (Sixty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1991**. It conferred a special status on the **Union Territory of Delhi**, designating it as the **National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi**.
 
• As per this article, the **Administrator** of the **National Capital Territory of Delhi**, appointed under **Article 239**, shall be designated as the **Lieutenant Governor**.
 
• The article provided for the creation of a **Legislative Assembly** for the **NCT of Delhi**, the members of which are chosen by **direct election** from territorial constituencies in the **Union Territory**.
 
• The **Legislative Assembly** has the power to make laws for the whole or any part of the **NCT of Delhi** with respect to any of the matters enumerated in the **State List** or **Concurrent List**, except for three specific subjects: **Public Order**, **Police**, and **Land**.
 
• These provisions officially came into force on **February 1, 1992**, marking a significant shift in the administrative and political structure of the capital city of **India**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 239AB**: This article deals with the **failure of constitutional machinery** in the **NCT of Delhi**. It allows the **President**, on receiving a report from the **Lieutenant Governor**, to suspend the operation of any provision of **Article 239AA** if the administration of the territory cannot be carried on in accordance with the law.
 
• **Article 239**: This is the general provision for the **administration of Union Territories**. It states that every **Union Territory** shall be administered by the **President** acting, to such extent as he thinks fit, through an administrator appointed by him with such **designation** as he may specify.
 
• **Article 239A**: This article was inserted by the **Constitution (Fourteenth Amendment) Act, 1962**, to create local **Legislatures** or **Council of Ministers** or both for certain **Union Territories** like **Puducherry**.
 
• **Article 239B**: Grants the **Administrator** of certain **Union Territories** the power to promulgate **ordinances** during the recess of the **Legislature**.
 
• The **69th Amendment Act** was based on the recommendations of the **S. Balakrishnan Committee**, which was set up in **1987** to look into the demands for statehood for **Delhi** and suggested a compromise of a **Legislative Assembly** with limited powers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Composition of the Assembly**: The **Legislative Assembly** of **Delhi** consists of **70 members**. The total number of seats is determined by **Parliament** by law.
 
• **Council of Ministers**: **Article 239AA(4)** provides for a **Council of Ministers** consisting of not more than **10%** of the total number of members in the **Legislative Assembly** (which equals **7 ministers**, including the **Chief Minister**), to aid and advise the **Lieutenant Governor** in the exercise of his functions.
 
• **Difference of Opinion**: In case of a difference of opinion between the **Lieutenant Governor** and his **Ministers** on any matter, the **Lieutenant Governor** shall refer it to the **President** for decision and act according to the decision given by the **President**.
 
• **Government of NCT of Delhi (Amendment) Act, 2021**: This recent amendment further clarified that the expression "**Government**" referred to in any law to be made by the **Legislative Assembly** shall mean the **Lieutenant Governor**, thereby increasing the discretionary powers of the **LG**.
 
• The **NCT of Delhi** is unique because, unlike other **Union Territories** (except **Puducherry** and **Jammu and Kashmir**), it has its own elected **Government** while remaining under the ultimate control of the **Union Government** through the **Ministry of Home Affairs**.

questions.question: A and B start running on a circular track of length 900 m. A runs at 225 m/min and B at 180 m/min. Every time A overtakes B, both reduce their speeds by 5% of their then speeds before continuing. After how many minutes (correct to two decimal places) does A overtake B for the 3rd time?
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

⇒ Relative speed initially = 225 − 180 = 45 m/min

⇒ Time for 1st overtake = 900 / 45 = 20 min

⇒ Speeds reduce by 5% each time ⇒ relative speed also × 0.95

⇒ Times form GP: 20, 20/0.95, 20/(0.95)²

⇒ Total time = 20 + 21.05 + 22.16 = 63.21 min

**∴ Answer = 63.21**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Track = 900 m

⇒ Speeds: A = 225, B = 180

**Formula:** Time = Distance / Relative Speed

⇒ 1st overtake:

⇒ Relative speed = 225 − 180 = 45

⇒ t₁ = 900 / 45 = 20 min

⇒ After 1st overtake speeds reduce:

⇒ A = 225 × 0.95 = 213.75

⇒ B = 180 × 0.95 = 171

⇒ Relative speed = 42.75

⇒ t₂ = 900 / 42.75 = 21.05 min

⇒ After 2nd overtake speeds reduce again:

⇒ A = 213.75 × 0.95 = 203.06

⇒ B = 171 × 0.95 = 162.45

⇒ Relative speed = 40.61

⇒ t₃ = 900 / 40.61 = 22.16 min

⇒ Total time = 20 + 21.05 + 22.16 = 63.21 min

**∴ Final Answer = 63.21**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

**Relative Speed:** Difference of speeds for same direction

**Circular Track:** Overtake when relative distance = track length

**Successive Reduction:** New speed = old speed × factor

**GP Insight:** Time increases as speed decreases proportionally

questions.question: Under the Citizenship Act, 1955, which section governs the grant of citizenship when a new territory becomes part of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Section 7**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Section 7** of the **Citizenship Act, 1955**, specifically addresses the "Incorporation of Territory." It stipulates that if any foreign territory becomes a part of **India**, the **Central Government** has the authority to specify which persons from that territory shall be recognized as **citizens of India**.
 
• Under this provision, the notification of citizenship is issued by the government through an order published in the **Official Gazette**. This ensures a legal transition for the inhabitants of the newly annexed or merged land.
 
• A primary historical example of the application of **Section 7** occurred when **Pondicherry** (now **Puducherry**) became part of the Indian Union. The Government issued the **Citizenship (Pondicherry) Order, 1962**, to grant Indian citizenship to the residents of that territory.
 
• The power granted under this section is absolute for the **Central Government**, allowing it to determine the **date** from which such persons shall become citizens based on their connection with the incorporated territory.
 
• This section is distinct from other modes of acquisition because it does not require individual applications or specific residency periods like **naturalization** or **registration**; it is a collective grant of citizenship based on **sovereign territorial change**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Section 5 (Citizenship by Registration):** This section allows the **Central Government** to register any person (not being an illegal migrant) as a citizen of India if they belong to certain categories. For instance, a person of **Indian origin** who is ordinarily resident in India for **7 years** before making an application can apply under this section.
 
• **Section 6 (Citizenship by Naturalization):** This pertains to foreigners who have resided in India for a specific duration. The applicant must have resided in India or been in **Government Service** for at least **12 months** immediately preceding the date of application, and for **11 years** out of the preceding **14 years**.
 
• **Section 9 (Termination of Citizenship):** This section mandates the automatic **termination** of Indian citizenship if a citizen of India voluntarily acquires the citizenship of another **country**. **India** does not permit **dual citizenship**, except for the **Overseas Citizen of India (OCI)** scheme which provides limited rights.
 
• **The Citizenship Act, 1955:** This is the comprehensive **Act** passed by the **Parliament** to provide for the acquisition and determination of Indian citizenship. It has been amended several times, most notably in **1986**, **1992**, **2003**, **2005**, **2015**, and **2019**.
 
• **Constitutional Framework:** While **Articles 5 to 11** of the **Constitution of India** deal with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution (**26 January 1950**), **Article 11** specifically empowers **Parliament** to make any provision regarding the acquisition and termination of citizenship.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Modes of Acquisition:** The **1955 Act** prescribes **five** ways to acquire citizenship: **Birth** (Section 3), **Descent** (Section 4), **Registration** (Section 5), **Naturalization** (Section 6), and **Incorporation of Territory** (Section 7).
 
• **Loss of Citizenship:** The **Act** mentions **three** ways an individual can lose their citizenship: **Renunciation** (voluntary giving up), **Termination** (by operation of law upon acquiring another nationality), and **Deprivation** (compulsory termination by the **Central Government** on grounds of fraud, disloyalty to the Constitution, or illegal conduct).
 
• **Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) 2019:** This **amendment** sought to provide a faster path to citizenship for persecuted minorities (**Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, and Christians**) from **Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan** who entered India on or before **31 December 2014**.
 
• **Nodal Ministry:** The **Ministry of Home Affairs** is the primary **organisation** responsible for matters related to citizenship and the implementation of the **Citizenship Act** in **India**.

questions.question: Which substance is the primary component of the reddish-brown coating formed on iron articles exposed to moist air?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Hydrated Iron (III) Oxide (Fe2O3·xH2O)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Rusting** is a specific type of **corrosion** that occurs when **iron** or iron-based alloys are exposed to **oxygen** and **moisture** (water) for a prolonged period.
 
• The **reddish-brown** coating formed during this process is chemically known as **Hydrated Iron (III) Oxide**, represented by the chemical formula **Fe2O3·xH2O**.
 
• The process of **rusting** is an **oxidation reaction** where iron metal loses electrons to oxygen in the presence of water. The overall chemical equation can be simplified as: **4Fe + 3O2 + 6H2O → 4Fe(OH)3**, which then dehydrates to form **Fe2O3·nH2O**.
 
• Unlike the protective oxide layers formed on metals like **aluminum**, rust is **porous** and **flaky**. It does not stick firmly to the surface, allowing the **oxidation** process to continue deep into the metal until the object is completely eaten away.
 
• For **rusting** to occur, both **air (oxygen)** and **moisture (water)** are essential requirements. If either is absent, the **reddish-brown** coating will not form on the **iron** article.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Methods of Prevention:**

 
 
• **Galvanization**: This is the process of applying a protective **zinc** coating to **iron** or **steel** to prevent **rusting**. **Zinc** is more reactive than iron and acts as a sacrificial anode.
 
• **Alloying**: Mixing **iron** with other elements like **chromium**, **nickel**, and **manganese** produces **stainless steel**, which is highly resistant to **corrosion**.
 
• **Painting and Greasing**: Applying a layer of **paint**, **oil**, or **grease** creates a physical barrier that prevents **oxygen** and **moisture** from coming into contact with the **metal** surface.
 
 
 
• **Other Iron Oxides:**
 
 
• **Iron (II) Oxide (FeO)**: Also known as **ferrous oxide**, it is a black-colored powder that is not the primary component of common **rust**.
 
• **Iron (II, III) Oxide (Fe3O4)**: Naturally occurring as the mineral **magnetite**, it is often found as a black scale on iron heated to high temperatures.
 
 
 
• **Factors Accelerating Rusting:**
 
 
• **Saltwater**: The presence of **electrolytes** (salts) in water increases the speed of the **electrochemical reaction** involved in **rusting**, which is why ships and coastal structures corrode faster.
 
• **Acidity**: Lower **pH** levels (acidic environments) increase the rate of **corrosion** by providing more **hydrogen ions** for the reaction.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Rusting** is considered a **chemical change** because it results in the formation of a new substance, **Hydrated Iron (III) Oxide**, which has different properties than the original **iron**.
 
• In the **Periodic Table**, **iron** (Fe) is a transition metal with the **atomic number 26**. It is one of the most widely used metals in **construction**, **machinery**, and **infrastructure** due to its strength.
 
• The **economic impact** of **corrosion** is significant; it is estimated that countries spend approximately **3% to 4%** of their **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** annually on replacing corroded parts and **prevention** measures.
 
• **Hydrated Iron (III) Oxide** is also used as a **pigment** in various industries, known as **Pigment Brown 6** or **Pigment Red 101**, due to its distinct **color** and stability.

questions.question: Simplify : ((525 times 525 times 525) + (321 times 321 times 321))/((525 times 525) - (525 times 321) + (321 times 321)) times (1)/((96 - 36))

[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

⇒ Use identity: a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²)

⇒ Numerator / denominator cancels ⇒ = (525 + 321)

⇒ = 846

⇒ Expression = 846 × 1/(96 − 36) = 846/60

⇒ = 14.1

**∴ Answer = 14.1**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

⇒ Numerator = a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²)

⇒ Denominator = (a² − ab + b²)

⇒ Cancel common term:

⇒ = a + b = 525 + 321 = 846

⇒ Remaining expression:

⇒ 846 × 1/(96 − 36)

⇒ = 846/60 = 14.1

**Cancellation:** Common terms simplify large expressions

**Speed Trick:** Always check identities before expanding

questions.question: The waves which can propagate in gases are:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Longitudinal Waves**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Longitudinal Waves**: These are **mechanical waves** in which the displacement of the medium is in the **same direction** as, or the **opposite direction** to, the direction of propagation of the wave. In **gases**, waves propagate through **compressions** (high pressure) and **rarefactions** (low pressure). Because gases possess **volume elasticity** (or **Bulk Modulus**), they can support the transmission of these pressure variations. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• **Transverse Waves**: In these waves, the particles of the medium move **perpendicular** to the direction of the wave's propagation. These waves require a medium with **shear strength** or **rigidity** to propagate. Since **gases** (and liquids) do not have **shear modulus** and cannot sustain a shearing force, transverse mechanical waves cannot propagate through the bulk of a gas. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• **Stationary Waves**: Also known as **standing waves**, these are formed by the **superposition** of two waves of the same **frequency** and **amplitude** traveling in opposite directions. While they can be observed in gas-filled cavities (like **organ pipes**), they do not "propagate" energy from one location to another in the traditional sense, as the wave profile remains **stationary** in space. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• **Gravity Waves**: These are waves generated in a **fluid medium** or at the **interface** between two media (like the atmosphere and ocean) when the **force of gravity** or **buoyancy** tries to restore equilibrium. While they exist in the **atmosphere**, they are distinct from the standard **acoustic waves** that propagate through the bulk of the gas via molecular collisions. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Properties of Sound in Gases**: **Sound** is the most common example of a **longitudinal wave**. The speed of sound in a gas depends on the **temperature**, **density**, and **molecular structure** of the gas. At **20 degrees Celsius**, the speed of sound in dry air is approximately **343 meters per second**.
 
• **Elasticity and Density**: The speed of a longitudinal wave in a medium is determined by the formula **v = √(B/ρ)**, where **B** is the **Bulk Modulus** and **ρ** is the **density**. Gases have a lower **Bulk Modulus** compared to solids and liquids, which is why sound generally travels **slower in gases** than in **water** or **steel**.
 
• **Newton's Formula and Laplace Correction**: In **1687**, **Sir Isaac Newton** assumed sound propagation in gases was an **isothermal process**. However, this led to inaccurate results. In **1816**, **Pierre-Simon Laplace** corrected this by treating the process as **adiabatic**, as heat does not have enough time to flow between compressions and rarefactions.
 
• **Electromagnetic Waves vs. Mechanical Waves**: It is important to note that **light** (an **electromagnetic wave**) is **transverse** in nature and can travel through a **vacuum** or gases. However, the question pertains to **mechanical waves** that require the gas molecules as a medium for propagation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Fluid Dynamics**: Since both **liquids and gases** are classified as **fluids**, they share the characteristic of being unable to support **transverse mechanical waves** in their interior. Only **longitudinal waves** can travel through the interior of any **fluid**.
 
• **Seismic Waves**: In **Geophysics**, **P-waves** (Primary waves) are **longitudinal** and can travel through the Earth's **liquid outer core**, whereas **S-waves** (Secondary waves) are **transverse** and cannot, which provides evidence for the **liquid nature** of the core.
 
• **Molecular Collisions**: In a gas, the **mean free path** (the average distance a molecule travels before colliding) affects the propagation of high-frequency **ultrasonic waves**. If the **wavelength** becomes comparable to the **mean free path**, the wave can no longer propagate effectively.

questions.question: Which constitutional amendment to the Indian Constitution added the term 'Socialist' to the Preamble?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**42nd Amendment, 1976**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **42nd Amendment Act**, passed in **1976**, is one of the most significant amendments in the history of the **Constitution of India**.
 
• It amended the **Preamble** of the Constitution to include three new terms: **Socialist**, **Secular**, and **Integrity**. Prior to this, India was described as a "Sovereign Democratic Republic." After the amendment, it became a "**Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic**."
 
• The addition of the word **Socialist** was intended to reflect the state's commitment to social and economic justice, aiming to reduce inequalities in income and status.
 
• This amendment was enacted during the **National Emergency** (**1975–1977**) under the government led by Prime Minister **Indira Gandhi**.
 
• The **42nd Amendment** is frequently referred to as the **"Mini-Constitution"** because of the massive number of changes it introduced to various parts of the Indian Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **44th Amendment Act, 1978**:

 
 
• Enacted by the **Janata Party** government led by **Morarji Desai** to nullify several controversial changes brought by the **42nd Amendment**.
 
• It removed the **Right to Property** from the list of **Fundamental Rights** and made it a **Legal Right** under **Article 300A**.
 
• It also ensured that the **Right to Life and Liberty** (**Article 21**) cannot be suspended even during an **Emergency**.
 
 
 
• **1st Amendment Act, 1951**:
 
 
• This was the first ever change to the Constitution, moved by **Jawaharlal Nehru**.
 
• It introduced the **Ninth Schedule** to protect land reform laws from being challenged in courts on the grounds of violating **Fundamental Rights**.
 
• It also placed "reasonable restrictions" on the **Freedom of Speech and Expression**.
 
 
 
• **26th Amendment Act, 1971**:
 
 
• This amendment was crucial in the history of post-independence India as it **abolished the Privy Purses**.
 
• It ended the recognition of the titles and special privileges previously enjoyed by the rulers of **former Princely States**.
 
 
 
• **Preamble of India**:
 
 
• The Preamble is based on the **"Objectives Resolution"** drafted and moved by **Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru** on **13 December 1946** and adopted by the **Constituent Assembly**.
 
• It serves as an introduction to the Constitution and outlines its basic philosophy and objectives.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Legal Status of the Preamble**: In the landmark **Kesavananda Bharati case** of **1973**, the **Supreme Court** ruled that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution and can be amended under **Article 368**, provided the **Basic Structure** of the Constitution remains intact.
 
• **Frequency of Amendments**: To date, the **Preamble** of the Indian Constitution has been amended **only once**, which was through the **42nd Amendment Act** of **1976**.
 
• **Swaran Singh Committee**: Most of the provisions of the **42nd Amendment** were based on the recommendations of the **Swaran Singh Committee**, which was appointed by the government to suggest changes to the Constitution.
 
• **Fundamental Duties**: Apart from changing the Preamble, the **42nd Amendment** also added **Part IV-A** containing **Article 51A**, which listed **10 Fundamental Duties** for Indian citizens.
 
• **Directive Principles**: It gave precedence to **Directive Principles of State Policy** over **Fundamental Rights** in certain cases and added new directives like **Equal Justice and Free Legal Aid** (**Article 39A**).

questions.question: How do Centre-State financial relations impact the governance in India?

options.text: By providing states with unlimited financial resources
By centralizing all tax revenues at the Centre
Through mechanisms like the Finance Commission that allocate resources
By eliminating the need for state budgets

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Through mechanisms like the Finance Commission that allocate resources**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 280** of the **Constitution of India** mandates the establishment of a **Finance Commission** every **five years** by the **President** to define the financial relations between the central government and the state governments.
 
• The primary function of the **Finance Commission** is to recommend the **distribution of net proceeds of taxes** between the **Union** and the **States** (vertical devolution) and the allocation between the states themselves (horizontal devolution). For the **15th Finance Commission**, the vertical devolution was set at **41%** for the states.
 
• Centre-State financial relations are governed by the **Seventh Schedule** of the **Constitution**, which divides taxing powers. While the **Centre** collects major taxes like **Income Tax** and **Corporation Tax**, the **States** have the power to levy taxes on **land revenue**, **state excise**, and **sales tax on petroleum and liquor**.
 
• Governance is impacted by these relations because states rely on **Central transfers** to fund social sector schemes. This fiscal federalism ensures that states with lower revenue-generating capacity receive higher **Grants-in-aid** to maintain administrative standards.
 
• Statement 1 is incorrect because financial resources are limited by the **FRBM Act, 2003**, and the overall **fiscal deficit** targets. Statement 2 is incorrect as states retain independent taxing powers under the **State List**. Statement 4 is incorrect because **Article 202** mandates every state to present its own **Annual Financial Statement** or **Budget**. ***Hence, the third option is the only correct mechanism described.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Goods and Services Tax (GST):** Introduced on **July 1, 2017**, through the **101st Constitutional Amendment Act**, it revolutionized financial relations by subsuming various central and state indirect taxes. The **GST Council**, chaired by the **Union Finance Minister**, serves as a joint forum for the Centre and States to decide on tax rates and exemptions.
 
• **Grants-in-Aid:** Under **Article 275**, the **Parliament** can provide financial assistance to specific states in need of help, particularly for the welfare of **Scheduled Tribes** or to improve administration in **Scheduled Areas**.
 
• **NITI Aayog:** Replacing the **Planning Commission** in **January 2015**, it acts as a premier policy think tank providing directional and policy inputs. It fosters **Cooperative Federalism** through structured support initiatives with the states on a continuous basis.
 
• **Borrowing Powers:** Under **Article 293**, the **State Executive** has the power to borrow money within the territory of **India** upon the security of the **Consolidated Fund of the State**, subject to limits set by the **State Legislature** and consent from the **Centre** if previous loans are outstanding.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **15th Finance Commission:** Chaired by **Shri N.K. Singh**, it used **2011 Census data** for the first time, moving away from **1971 data**, which significantly influenced the resource allocation based on **demographic performance** and **tax effort**.
 
• **Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS):** These are schemes where the funding is shared between the **Centre** and **States**, usually in a **60:40** ratio for general states and **90:10** for **North-Eastern** and **Himalayan States**.
 
• **Article 268 to 293:** These articles in **Part XII** of the **Constitution** deal with the distribution of revenues between the **Union** and the **States**, ensuring a balance of **fiscal powers**.
 
• **Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act:** This **2003** act sets targets for the government to reduce **fiscal deficits**. States are generally required to keep their fiscal deficit within **3%** of their **GSDP (Gross State Domestic Product)**.

questions.question: In an election between two candidates, 84% of the registered voters cast their votes and 20% of the votes polled were found invalid. Winning candidate got 58% of the valid votes and won the election by a margin of 336 votes. How many voters were registered?

⇒ 16% of V = 336 ⇒ V = 336 × 100 ÷ 16 = 2100

⇒ Valid = 80% of polled ⇒ Polled = 2100 ÷ 0.8 = 2625

⇒ Polled = 84% of registered ⇒ Registered = 2625 ÷ 0.84 = 3125

**∴ Answer = 3125**

⇒ 16% of valid votes = 336

⇒ Valid votes = 336 × 100 ÷ 16 = 2100

⇒ Valid = 80% of polled

questions.question: Which core component of Windows OS is responsible for handling low-level operations such as memory management and process scheduling?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Windows Kernel**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Windows Kernel** is the central core of the **Windows Operating System**, serving as the bridge between software applications and the physical **hardware** of the computer. It is responsible for critical low-level operations like **memory management** and **process scheduling**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• In terms of **memory management**, the kernel tracks every **memory location**, managing the transition between **Physical RAM** and **Virtual Memory** to ensure that each **process** has enough resources to execute without interfering with others.
 
• The **process scheduling** function of the kernel determines which **thread** or **process** receives **CPU** time and for how long. It uses complex **algorithms** to prioritize tasks, ensuring system stability and responsiveness for the **user**.
 
• The **Windows Kernel** operates in **Kernel Mode** (also known as **Ring 0**), which grants it unrestricted access to the **system hardware** and **CPU instructions**, protecting the system from crashes caused by faulty **user-level applications**.
 
• It also handles **Interrupt Management**, where it responds to signals from **hardware devices** like **keyboards**, **mice**, and **hard drives**, ensuring that the **processor** handles these events immediately and accurately.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Architecture Type:** The **Windows OS** utilizes a **Hybrid Kernel** architecture, which combines the speed of a **Monolithic Kernel** with the modularity of a **Microkernel**. This design started with **Windows NT** and continues through modern versions like **Windows 10** and **Windows 11**.
 
• **Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL):** A vital sub-component of the **Windows** executive, the **HAL** is a **software layer** that hides **hardware** differences from the rest of the **kernel**, allowing the **OS** to run on different **motherboards** and **chipsets** without major code changes.
 
• **I/O Management:** The kernel includes an **I/O Manager** that facilitates communication between **applications** and **device drivers**. It translates **read/write** requests into **I/O Request Packets (IRPs)** that the **hardware** can understand.
 
• **Security Reference Monitor (SRM):** This component within the kernel enforces **access control** and **security policies** on the **local system**, ensuring that **users** can only access **files** and **objects** they are authorized to use.
 
• **Registry Management:** While the **Registry** is a **database**, the kernel manages the **Configuration Manager**, which handles the **reading and writing** of **system settings** and **configuration data** during **boot time** and **runtime**.

questions.question: According to Census 2011, which of the following states showed a negative decadal population growth rate between 2001 and 2011?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Nagaland**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• According to the **Census 2011**, **Nagaland** was the only state in **India** to record a negative decadal population growth rate. Between the years **2001 and 2011**, its growth rate was approximately **-0.58%** (often rounded to **-0.6%**).
 
• This negative growth was a significant shift from the **1991-2001** census period, where **Nagaland** had reported an exceptionally high growth rate of **64.53%**. Experts suggest this anomaly was likely due to the correction of previous over-estimations and inflated figures in the **2001 Census**.
 
• The **Census 2011** was the **15th National Census** of the country since **1872** and the **7th** after Independence. It was conducted under the guidance of **C. Chandramouli**, the then **Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India**.
 
• In contrast to **Nagaland**, the state of **Meghalaya** recorded the highest decadal growth rate among all states at **27.9%**, followed by **Arunachal Pradesh** at **26%**.
 
• While **Nagaland** showed a decline, the state of **Kerala** recorded the lowest positive decadal growth rate among the states at **4.9%**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Population Growth in Other States (2001-2011):**

 
 
• **Gujarat:** This western state recorded a decadal growth rate of **19.3%**. **Gujarat** has consistently shown industrial and urban growth, contributing to its population dynamics.
 
• **Kerala:** Known for its high literacy and advanced social indicators, **Kerala** had a growth rate of **4.9%**. This was the lowest among the states (excluding **Nagaland**) and significantly lower than the national average.
 
• **Punjab:** The state of **Punjab** recorded a decadal growth rate of **13.9%**. It is one of the states where the growth rate remained lower than the overall Indian average.
 
• **National Average:** The overall decadal population growth rate of **India** during **2001-2011** was **17.7%**, a decrease from **21.5%** in the previous decade (**1991-2001**).
 
 
 
• **Significant Census 2011 Facts:**
 
 
• The slogan of the **2011 Census** was **"Our Census, Our Future"**.
 
• The total population of **India** as per the **2011 Census** was **1.21 billion** (approximately **121.08 crore**), making it the second most populous country at that time.
 
• **Uttar Pradesh** was identified as the most populous state, while **Sikkim** was the least populous state in **India**.
 
• **Thane** district in **Maharashtra** was the most populated district in the country.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Decadal Growth Rate:** It refers to the percentage of total population growth in a particular area (state/country) over a period of **10 years**. It is a vital indicator used by the government for resource allocation and policy planning.
 
• **Demographic Transition:** The decline in growth rates in states like **Kerala** and the negative growth in **Nagaland** indicate different stages of demographic transition. Lower growth rates are typically associated with higher **literacy rates**, better **healthcare**, and increased **urbanization**.
 
• **Gender Statistics:** In the **2011 Census**, the child sex ratio (**0-6 years**) saw a decline to **919**, which remains a critical concern for policymakers. The overall **sex ratio** in **India** was **943 females** per **1000 males**.
 
• **Literacy Rate:** The national literacy rate was recorded at **73%**. **Kerala** topped the list with a **94%** literacy rate, while **Bihar** was at the bottom with **61.8%**.
 
• **Administrative Units:** During the **2011 Census**, there were **28 states** and **7 Union Territories** (before the reorganization of **Jammu and Kashmir** and the merger of **Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu**).

questions.question: Which 2025 event by the United Nations highlights that member states continue to ratify a variety of multilateral treaties across human rights, the environment, penal law, and the law of the sea, among others?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2025 Treaty Event**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **2025 Treaty Event** is a high-level **United Nations** event held annually, typically during the opening of the **General Debate** of the **General Assembly** in **September 2025** in **New York**. It serves as a dedicated platform for member states to demonstrate their commitment to the international legal framework.
 
• The primary objective of the event is to encourage the **universal participation** of member states in **multilateral treaties** deposited with the **Secretary-General**. These treaties span a wide range of global issues, including **human rights**, **disarmament**, **environmental protection**, **penal law**, and the **law of the sea**.
 
• The tradition of the Treaty Event was established in the **year 2000** during the **Millennium Summit** to promote the rule of law at the international level. Since its inception, it has resulted in thousands of treaty actions, including **signatures**, **ratifications**, and **accessions**.
 
• For the **2025** cycle, the **United Nations** highlights specific **multilateral treaties** that address contemporary global challenges, such as the **Agreement under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ Agreement)**.
 
• The event provides a unique opportunity for **Heads of State** and **Heads of Government** to deposit their instruments of ratification in a high-profile setting, signaling their country's adherence to **international law** and **global standards**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **UN Ocean Conference 2025:** This conference is scheduled to be held in **Nice**, **France**, in **June 2025**. It is co-hosted by **France** and **Costa Rica** and focuses specifically on **Sustainable Development Goal 14 (Life Below Water)** to support the conservation and sustainable use of the oceans, seas, and marine resources.
 
• **Paris Climate Summit (COP30):** The **30th** session of the **Conference of the Parties (COP30)** to the **UNFCCC** is expected to take place in **Belém**, **Brazil**, in **November 2025**. This event is critical for the **Paris Agreement** as it will involve the submission of new **Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)** by member states to tackle climate change.
 
• **UN Biodiversity Summit:** While **COP16** of the **Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)** occurs in **2024**, the year **2025** remains significant for implementing the **Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework**, which aims to protect **30%** of the planet's land and oceans by **2030**.
 
• **Treaty Section of the OLA:** The **Office of Legal Affairs (OLA)** of the **United Nations**, specifically the **Treaty Section**, is responsible for the technical and legal processing of all treaty actions during the event. They maintain the **United Nations Treaty Series**, which contains over **250,000** treaties and related actions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Role of the Secretary-General:** The **United Nations Secretary-General** acts as the **depositary** for more than **600** multilateral treaties. In this role, the **Secretary-General** ensures that all legal formalities regarding the entry into force and implementation of these treaties are strictly followed.
 
• **Legal Terminologies:** It is important to distinguish between **Signature** (a preliminary endorsement of a treaty), **Ratification** (the formal process by which a state confirms its consent to be bound, usually involving domestic legislative approval), and **Accession** (the act by which a state joins a treaty that has already been negotiated and signed by other states).
 
• **Law of the Sea:** The **United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)**, often described as the "constitution for the oceans," remains a central pillar of the **Treaty Event**, especially with the recent focus on the **BBNJ Agreement**, which was adopted in **June 2023** and opened for signature in **September 2023**.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about the role of Cabinet Ministers in India?

options.text: They are not involved in policy decisions.
They only assist other ministers in their duties.
They head important ministries like Home, Defence, and Finance.
They do not attend Cabinet meetings.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**They head important ministries like Home, Defence, and Finance**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Cabinet Ministers** are senior members of the **Council of Ministers** and hold independent charge of specific **ministries** or **departments** of the **Government of India**.
 
• They head the most crucial and strategically important portfolios such as **Home**, **Defence**, **Finance**, **External Affairs**, and **Railways**. ***Hence, the statement "They head important ministries like Home, Defence, and Finance" is correct.***
 
• They are the core **policy-making body** of the central government, responsible for deliberating and deciding upon major **national policies**, **legislations**, and **administrative matters**. Therefore, the statement "They are not involved in policy decisions" is **incorrect**.
 
• **Cabinet Ministers** are the only category of ministers who have a legal right to attend **Cabinet meetings**, which are presided over by the **Prime Minister**. Consequently, the statement "They do not attend Cabinet meetings" is **incorrect**.
 
• The role of assisting senior ministers is typically performed by **Ministers of State** or **Deputy Ministers**, not by the Cabinet Ministers themselves. This makes the statement "They only assist other ministers in their duties" **incorrect**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Structure of the Council of Ministers:** The **Union Council of Ministers** consists of three ranks: **Cabinet Ministers**, **Ministers of State**, and **Deputy Ministers**. The total number of ministers cannot exceed **15%** of the total strength of the **Lok Sabha**, as per the **91st Amendment Act, 2003**.
 
• **Constitutional Status:** **Article 74** of the **Constitution of India** provides for a **Council of Ministers** with the **Prime Minister** at the head to aid and advise the **President**. **Article 75** deals with the appointment, tenure, responsibility, and salaries of the ministers.
 
• **Collective Responsibility:** Under **Article 75(3)**, the Council of Ministers is **collectively responsible** to the **Lok Sabha**. This means that if a **no-confidence motion** is passed against one minister, the entire council must resign.
 
• **Definition of Cabinet:** While the word 'Cabinet' was not originally detailed in the Constitution, it was inserted into **Article 352** via the **44th Amendment Act, 1978**. It defines the Cabinet as the council consisting of the **Prime Minister** and other ministers of **Cabinet rank**.
 
• **Selection and Appointment:** Ministers are appointed by the **President** on the advice of the **Prime Minister**. A person who is not a member of either **House of Parliament** can also be appointed as a minister, but they must become a member of either **Lok Sabha** or **Rajya Sabha** within **6 months**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Cabinet Committees:** These are specialized units like the **Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC)** and the **Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA)** that handle specific issues. They are usually chaired by the **Prime Minister** and consist mainly of **Cabinet Ministers**.
 
• **Role of the Prime Minister:** The **Prime Minister** is the "primus inter pares" (first among equals) and determines the size of the **Cabinet** and the **portfolios** allocated to each minister.
 
• **Cabinet Secretariat:** This office provides **secretarial assistance** to the Cabinet and its committees. It is headed by the **Cabinet Secretary**, who is the **topmost civil servant** in India and acts as the chairman of the **Senior Selection Board**.
 
• **Advisory Function:** The advice tendered by the **Council of Ministers** to the **President** is binding after the **42nd Amendment Act, 1976** (subject to the President's power to ask for reconsideration once under the **44th Amendment**).

questions.question: Under which of the following categories do headphones fall?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• An **Output Device** is a piece of **computer hardware** equipment used to communicate the results of data processing carried out by an information processing system (such as a computer) to the outside world. Headphones fall strictly into this category as they receive **electronic signals** and convert them into **audible sound waves**. ***Hence, the statement that headphones are an output device is correct.***
 
• The primary **function** of headphones is to provide a private **audio experience** for the user. They act as **transducers**, converting **electrical energy** from a device like a **smartphone**, **laptop**, or **MP3 player** into **acoustic energy**.
 
• Unlike **speakers**, which are also output devices designed for multiple listeners, headphones are localized output devices intended for a **single user**. They allow for the consumption of **multimedia content** without disturbing others in the **vicinity**.
 
• In the context of the **Human-Computer Interaction (HCI)**, headphones represent the **auditory output channel**. They are essential for **tasks** involving **sound monitoring**, **video editing**, and **gaming**, where **directional audio** and **clarity** are required.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **History and Origin:** The first modern headphones were developed in **1910** by **Nathaniel Baldwin**, who manufactured them in his **kitchen** and sold them to the **United States Navy**. They were initially used for **radio communication** before becoming a **consumer electronic** staple.
 
• **Types of Headphones:**
 
 
• **Over-ear (Circumaural):** These have large **earcups** that surround the entire ear, offering excellent **sound isolation**.
 
• **On-ear (Supra-aural):** These sit directly on the **outer ear** and are generally **lighter** and more **portable**.
 
• **In-ear (Earbuds/IEMs):** These are inserted into the **ear canal**, making them the most **compact** option, often used with **mobile devices**.
 
 
 
• **Input vs. Output Devices:** While an **Output Device** (like headphones or a monitor) displays or emits processed data, an **Input Device** (like a **keyboard** or **mouse**) sends **data** and **control signals** to the computer for processing.
 
• **Hybrid Devices:** Some devices, known as **headsets**, combine both **output** (headphones) and **input** (a **microphone**). These are widely used in **telecommunications**, **customer service**, and **online gaming**.
 
• **Storage and Calculation Devices:** A **Storage Device** (like a **Hard Disk Drive** or **SSD**) is used for **permanent data retention**, while a **Calculator Device** (like a **microprocessor** or **ALU**) is responsible for performing **arithmetic** and **logic operations**. Headphones perform neither of these **functions**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Connectivity:** Headphones can connect to devices via **wired** connections (using a **3.5mm jack**, **USB-C**, or **Lightning port**) or **wireless** technologies such as **Bluetooth** (versions **5.0** and above are currently standard).
 
• **Technical Specifications:** Key **metrics** for headphones include **Impedance** (measured in **Ohms**), **Frequency Response** (typically **20Hz to 20kHz**), and **Sensitivity** (measured in **dB/mW**). These factors determine the **audio quality** and the **power** required to drive the device.
 
• **Applications:** Beyond entertainment, headphones are used in **specialized fields** such as **Aviation** for **pilot communication**, in **Medical Science** for **audiometry tests**, and in **Military** operations for **sonar monitoring**.
 
• **Features:** Modern output devices in this category often feature **Active Noise Cancellation (ANC)**, which uses **microphones** to pick up external **noise** and create **anti-noise** to cancel it out, providing a **clearer output**.

questions.question: Which of the following objectives is mentioned in Article 39 of the Indian Constitution?

options.text: To ensure equal justice and provide free legal aid
To organise agriculture and animal husbandry
To promote equal pay for equal work for both men and women

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To promote equal pay for equal work for both men and women**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 39** of the **Constitution of India** contains certain principles of policy to be followed by the **State**. It is a part of the **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)**, which are mentioned in **Part IV**.
 
• Specifically, **Article 39(d)** mandates that the State shall direct its policy towards securing that there is **equal pay for equal work** for both **men and women**. ***Hence, the statement in the correct option is mentioned in Article 39.***
 
• Other provisions under **Article 39** include:
 
 
• **Article 39(a)**: Citizens, men and women equally, have the right to an adequate **means of livelihood**.
 
• **Article 39(b)**: Ownership and control of the **material resources** of the community are distributed to subserve the **common good**.
 
• **Article 39(c)**: The operation of the economic system does not result in the **concentration of wealth** and means of production to the common detriment.
 
• **Article 39(e)**: The health and strength of workers and the **tender age of children** are not abused.
 
• **Article 39(f)**: Children are given opportunities and facilities to develop in a healthy manner. This clause was modified by the **42nd Amendment Act of 1976**.
 
 
 
• These principles are fundamental in the **governance** of the country, and it shall be the duty of the **State** to apply these principles in making **laws**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)**:

 
 
• The **DPSP** are enumerated in **Articles 36 to 51** of the **Indian Constitution**.
 
• The concept was borrowed from the **Irish Constitution** of **1937**, which had copied it from the **Spanish Constitution**.
 
• They are **non-justiciable** in nature, meaning they are not legally enforceable by the **courts** for their violation.
 
 
 
• **Article 39A (Equal Justice and Free Legal Aid)**:
 
 
• The objective "To ensure equal justice and provide free legal aid" is mentioned in **Article 39A**, not **Article 39**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect in the context of Article 39.***
 
• This article was added by the **42nd Constitutional Amendment Act** in **1976** to promote justice on the basis of **equal opportunity**.
 
 
 
• **Article 40 (Organisation of Village Panchayats)**:
 
 
• The objective "To organise village panchayats" is mentioned in **Article 40**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect in the context of Article 39.***
 
• It directs the State to endow them with such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to function as units of **self-government**.
 
 
 
• **Article 48 (Organisation of Agriculture and Animal Husbandry)**:
 
 
• The objective "To organise agriculture and animal husbandry" is mentioned in **Article 48**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect in the context of Article 39.***
 
• It directs the State to organize these sectors on **modern and scientific lines** and take steps for preserving and improving the breeds of **cattle**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Supreme Court of India** has often relied on **Article 39(d)** to interpret labor laws and ensure that **gender discrimination** in wages is eliminated.
 
• The **Equal Remuneration Act, 1976** was enacted by the **Parliament** to give effect to the constitutional provision of **equal pay for equal work**.

questions.question: According to early Buddhist literature, how many gāmas (villages) were said to exist in the kingdom of Magadha during the reign of King Bimbisāra?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**80,000**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• According to the **Mahāvagga**, which is a significant part of the **Vinaya Pitaka** (one of the three baskets of early **Buddhist literature**), it is mentioned that the kingdom of **Magadha** comprised **80,000** villages (**gāmas**) during the reign of King **Bimbisāra**.
 
• King **Bimbisāra** is recorded to have summoned an assembly of the **gāmanis** (village headmen) from each of these **80,000** villages to address administrative matters and to encourage them to seek the guidance of the **Buddha**.
 
• This large **numerical value** of **80,000** highlights the vast extent, dense population, and organized **administrative structure** of the **Magadha** empire in the **6th century BCE**.
 
• The mention of such a specific number in **Buddhist texts** serves to emphasize **Bimbisāra's** status as a powerful **monarch** and his deep connection with the **Buddhist sangha**. *Hence, the option stating 80,000 is correct.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **King Bimbisāra:** He ruled **Magadha** from approximately **544 BCE to 492 BCE** and was the founder of the **Haryanka Dynasty**. He was a contemporary of **Gautama Buddha** and was known for his policy of **expansion** through **conquest** and **matrimonial alliances**.
 
• **Matrimonial Alliances:** To strengthen **Magadha**, **Bimbisāra** married princesses from powerful neighboring states, including **Kosala Devi** (sister of King Prasenajit of **Kosala**), **Chellana** (a Lichchhavi princess from **Vaishali**), and **Khema** (princess of **Madra** in Punjab).
 
• **The Title 'Seniya':** He was the first Indian king to maintain a **standing army**, which earned him the title of **Seniya** (one who has an army). This military strength was crucial for his **annexation** of the kingdom of **Anga**.
 
• **Capital City:** His capital was **Girivraja**, later known as **Rajagriha** (modern-day Rajgir in **Bihar**). The city was strategically fortified by **five hills**, making it a secure center for the growing **Magadhan** power.
 
• **Religious Patronage:** While **Bimbisāra** was a great devotee of the **Buddha** and donated the **Veluvana bamboo grove** to the **Sangha**, historical accounts also suggest he showed respect toward **Jainism** and other contemporary sects.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Rise of Magadha:** The kingdom of **Magadha** became the most powerful **Mahajanapada** due to its **geographical location** near **iron ore** mines and fertile land in the **Gangetic plains**, which provided **agricultural surplus** and advanced **weaponry**.
 
• **Administrative Setup:** The **Magadhan** administration under **Bimbisāra** was highly efficient. He appointed various officials known as **Mahamattas** to oversee different functions like **executive**, **judicial**, and **military** affairs.
 
• **Succession:** **Bimbisāra** was eventually succeeded by his son, **Ajatashatru**, who according to **Buddhist** and **Jain** traditions, imprisoned his father to seize the **throne**. **Ajatashatru** continued the **expansionist** policies of his father, further consolidating **Magadha's** dominance.
 
• **Early Buddhist Texts:** The **Vinaya Pitaka**, from which this data is derived, primarily deals with the **rules of conduct** for monks but provides invaluable **historical data** regarding the **socio-political** conditions of ancient **India**.

questions.question: Barren Island, which witnessed two eruptions in 2025, is situated in which Union Territory of India?

options.text: Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Andaman & Nicobar Islands**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Barren Island** is located in the **Andaman Sea** and is politically part of the **Andaman and Nicobar Islands**, a **Union Territory** of **India**.
 
• It is famously known as the only **active volcano** along a chain of volcanoes from **Sumatra** to **Myanmar** and is the only active one in the **Indian subcontinent** and **South Asia**.
 
• The island is situated approximately **138 kilometers** (86 miles) northeast of the territory's capital, **Port Blair**.
 
• As mentioned in the question context, the volcano witnessed **two eruptions** in the year **2025**, continuing its history of frequent activity since the **1991** eruption, which ended a **150-year** period of dormancy.
 
• The island is currently **uninhabited** by humans, though it supports a small population of **feral goats**, birds, and crabs that have adapted to the harsh volcanic environment.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Andaman & Nicobar Islands**: This **Union Territory** consists of **572 islands**, of which only about **38** are inhabited. It is divided into three districts: **North and Middle Andaman**, **South Andaman**, and **Nicobar**.
 
• **Geological Setting**: The **Barren Island** volcano is part of the **Neogene-Quaternary volcanic arc**. It lies near the boundary of the **Indian Plate** and the **Burmese Microplate**, a subduction zone that creates significant **seismic and volcanic activity**.
 
• **Narcondam Island**: Another volcanic island in the **Andaman Sea**, located about **150 km** north of Barren Island. Unlike Barren Island, **Narcondam** is classified as a **dormant volcano** and is a **UNESCO World Heritage site** due to its unique biodiversity, including the **Narcondam Hornbill**.
 
• **Lakshadweep**: For contrast, this **Union Territory** on the western coast of **India** consists of **coral atolls** rather than volcanic islands. It is the smallest Union Territory of India by area.
 
• **Other Options**: **Puducherry** and **Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu** are coastal or land-locked territories on the mainland and do not contain any volcanic formations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Eruption History**: The first recorded eruption of **Barren Island** occurred in **1787**. After several eruptions in the **18th and 19th centuries**, it remained quiet until **1991**. Major recent activities were also recorded in **2005**, **2017**, and notably in **2025**.
 
• **Topography**: The volcano reaches an elevation of **354 meters** above sea level, but it is actually the summit of a much larger **submarine volcano** rising from the **ocean floor** at a depth of nearly **2,250 meters**.
 
• **Tourism and Accessibility**: Landing on **Barren Island** is strictly prohibited for security and safety reasons. However, tourists can view the island from **chartered boats** or **seaplanes** operated from **Port Blair** under specific **government guidelines**.
 
• **Scientific Monitoring**: The **Geological Survey of India (GSI)** and the **National Institute of Oceanography (NIO)** closely monitor the island's activities to study **plate tectonics** and **volcanology** in the **Bay of Bengal** region.

questions.question: Which law of Mendel explains the separation of alleles during gamete formation?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Law of Segregation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Law of Segregation**, also known as **Mendel's First Law**, states that during the production of gametes, the two copies of each hereditary factor (alleles) segregate so that offspring acquire one factor from each parent.
 
• This law explains that in a **diploid** organism, the two alleles for a specific trait separate during the process of **meiosis** (specifically **Anaphase I**), ensuring that each gamete (egg or sperm) carries only one allele for each gene.
 
• **Gregor Mendel** formulated this principle after performing **monohybrid cross** experiments with **Pisum sativum** (garden pea) plants in the **mid-19th century**, specifically around **1865**.
 
• The law is based on the observation that recessive traits, which might be "hidden" in the **F1 generation**, reappear in the **F2 generation** in a specific **3:1** phenotypic ratio. ***Hence, the statement regarding the separation of alleles is explained by the Law of Segregation.***
 
• This principle is fundamental to understanding how genetic diversity is maintained and how traits are passed from one generation to the next without blending.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Law of Dominance**:

 
 
• This law states that in a **heterozygote**, one allele will conceal the presence of another allele for the same characteristic. Rather than both alleles contributing to a phenotype, the **dominant allele** will be expressed exclusively.
 
• The **recessive allele** will remain "latent" but will be transmitted to offspring in the same manner as the dominant allele. The recessive trait will only be expressed by offspring that have **two copies** of this allele (**homozygous recessive**).
 
 
 
• **Law of Independent Assortment**:
 
 
• Known as **Mendel's Second Law**, it states that the alleles of two (or more) different genes get sorted into gametes independently of one another.
 
• In other words, the allele a gamete receives for one gene does not influence the allele received for another gene. This is typically observed in **dihybrid crosses** and applies to genes located on different **chromosomes**.
 
• This law results in a typical **9:3:3:1** phenotypic ratio in the **F2 generation**.
 
 
 
• **Gregor Mendel**:
 
 
• Known as the **"Father of Genetics"**, he was an Austrian monk who conducted his famous experiments in the **Brno** monastery (now in the **Czech Republic**) between **1856** and **1863**.
 
• He tracked **7** distinct characteristics of pea plants, including seed shape, seed color, flower color, and stem height.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Exceptions to Mendel's Laws**:

 
 
• **Incomplete Dominance**: Where the phenotype of the offspring is a blend of the parents (e.g., pink flowers in **Mirabilis jalapa** from red and white parents).
 
• **Codominance**: Where both alleles are expressed equally in the phenotype, such as the **ABO blood group** system in humans.
 
• **Linkage**: Genes that are located very close to each other on the same **chromosome** tend to be inherited together, which violates the Law of Independent Assortment.
 
 
 
• **Genotype vs. Phenotype**:
 
 
• **Genotype** refers to the **genetic makeup** (e.g., **Tt**), while **Phenotype** refers to the **physical appearance** (e.g., **Tall**).
 
• A **Punnett Square** is a common tool used to predict the genotypes and phenotypes of offspring based on the Law of Segregation.

questions.question: Which of the following methods was characteristically adopted by the Moderates during the early phase of the Indian national movement?

options.text: Boycott of foreign goods and institutions

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Constitutional reforms**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Moderates** (Early Nationalists) dominated the **Indian National Congress** from its inception in **1885** until **1905**. Their primary method was **Constitutional reforms**, which involved working within the legal framework provided by the **British Government** to seek gradual changes. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• The **Swadeshi Movement** was characteristically adopted by the **Extremists** (Radicals) following the **Partition of Bengal** in **1905**. It involved the use of indigenous goods and was a shift toward more radical mass mobilization. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• The **Promotion of Vedic education** was a feature of socio-religious reform movements, most notably the **Arya Samaj** founded by **Dayanand Saraswati** in **1875**. While it influenced national pride, it was not the characteristic political method of the **Moderates**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• The **Boycott of foreign goods and institutions** became a major political tool during the **Anti-Partition Agitation** (1905-1908) and was championed by **Extremist** leaders like **Lala Lajpat Rai** and **Bal Gangadhar Tilak**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***
 
• **Moderates** believed in the **British** sense of justice and fair play. They utilized the policy of the **Three Ps**: **Petition**, **Prayer**, and **Protest** to convey their demands to the **United Kingdom** government.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Prominent Moderate Leaders**:

 
 
• **Dadabhai Naoroji**: Known as the **Grand Old Man of India**, he was a three-time president of the **Indian National Congress** and the first **Indian** to be elected to the **British House of Commons** in **1892**.
 
• **Gopal Krishna Gokhale**: He founded the **Servants of India Society** in **1905** and was considered the political guru of **Mahatma Gandhi**.
 
• **Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee**: He served as the first president of the **Indian National Congress** during the **Bombay** session in **1885**.
 
• **Surendranath Banerjea**: Often called the **Indian Burke**, he founded the **Indian National Association** in **1876**.
 
 
 
• **Economic Critique of Colonialism**:
 
 
• One of the greatest contributions of the **Moderates** was the **Drain of Wealth** theory, primarily formulated by **Dadabhai Naoroji** in his book **"Poverty and Un-British Rule in India"**.
 
• They argued that **India's** poverty was not natural but was a result of the **British** policy of exporting **Indian** resources to **England** without any equivalent return.
 
 
 
• **Political Demands**:
 
 
• They demanded the **Indianization** of higher grades of administrative services through simultaneous **Civil Services Examinations** in **India** and **England**.
 
• They sought the expansion and reform of **Legislative Councils**, leading to the enactment of the **Indian Councils Act of 1892**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **The Safety Valve Theory**: It was suggested by some historians that the **Indian National Congress** was formed by **A.O. Hume** in **1885** under **Lord Dufferin** to provide a "safety valve" for the release of **Indian** discontent to prevent another revolt like **1857**.
 
• **The Shift in 1905**: The **Moderates'** failure to achieve significant concessions from the **British** and the reactionary policies of **Lord Curzon** led to the rise of the **Extremist** faction within the **Congress**, eventually leading to the **Surat Split** in **1907**.
 
• **Methods of Agitation**: While the **Moderates** used **memorandums** and **resolutions**, they avoided mass strikes or **passive resistance**, fearing that the **British** would suppress the nascent movement with **force**.
 
• **Administrative Reforms**: They campaigned for the separation of the **Judiciary** from the **Executive** and the repeal of the **Arms Act of 1878** and the **Vernacular Press Act**.
